item.title: Former Texas high school teacher arrested after probe into inappropriate student relationship
item.description: Holly Adams, an Angleton High School teacher, faces charges of tampering with evidence and furnishing alcohol to minors after a year-long investigation.
item.content:encoded:
A former Texas schoolteacher was arrested Tuesday amid allegations of inappropriate relationships with students, nearly one year after authorities began investigating her.

Holly Adams, who taught at Angleton High School near Houston, is charged with one count of tampering with evidence and two counts of purchasing or furnishing alcohol to a minor, the Brazoria County Sheriff's Office said.

The probe began after a student told school staff that Adams was having an inappropriate relationship with a former student, KTRK-TV reported.

TEXAS SUBSTITUTE TEACHER ACCUSED OF IMPROPER RELATIONSHIP WITH STUDENT, ALARMING PARENTS

The student told school officials that the victim FaceTime-called him over the summer from a bedroom in Adams' house and that the bed was covered in nude photos of her, according to the news outlet. Another image depicted Adams and the former student cuddling, the report states.

Adams reportedly invited students to her home to perform chores, and she allegedly admitted to speaking with three members of the school baseball team on Snapchat.

HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER WHO ALLEGEDLY HAD SEX WITH STUDENT IN CLOSET NOW FACES CHARGES INVOLVING MORE TEENS

Many female teachers who sexually abuse male students sometimes convice themselves that the relationship is legitimate, said Gail Saltz, MD, Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical College.

"They're more likely to be psychologically both grooming their victim, but also what's called self grooming," Saltz told Fox News Digital. "They are convincing themselves that what they are doing is having an intimate, romantic relationship that is benefiting the victim as well."

Saltz noted that the damage done to the male students is just as damaging as female victims.

"It is easily as damaging in terms of, you've been abused by an adult. And that adult took advantage of your trust," she said. "That violated boundaries that you weren't ready for."

Adams was taken to the Brazoria County Detention Center and released on a $26,000 bond the same day. She no longer works for the Angleton Independent School District, a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff's office.

item.title: Massachusetts high court blocks city from displaying Catholic saint statues honoring first responders
item.description: The Becket Fund vowed to fight after Massachusetts' highest court blocked Quincy from installing St. Michael and St. Florian statues at city hall.
item.content:encoded:
Massachusetts' highest court has blocked a city from installing two towering Catholic saint statues honoring police officers and firefighters outside a new public safety headquarters, ruling the monuments could improperly signal government support for one religion.

The Aug. 20 ruling upheld an October 2025 lower court decision that temporarily blocked the city from installing two 10-foot statues of St. Michael the Archangel, the patron saint of police officers, and St. Florian, the patron saint of firefighters.

The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, which is representing the city of Quincy, told Fox News Digital the legal battle is not over.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

"This ruling is disappointing but is only preliminary," Joe Davis, senior counsel at Becket and lead attorney for the city of Quincy, told Fox News Digital. "Quincy chose these statues to honor the courage and sacrifice of its firefighters and police. 

"The city should not have to hide public art simply because some people may think of religion when they see it. As the court noted today, this is not the final word for these statues, and we will continue defending Quincy’s right to honor its heroes."

Critics contend that placing religious figures outside a government building would violate the Massachusetts Constitution's protections on religious neutrality.

The controversy began after The Patriot Ledger reported that Quincy planned to install the two statues outside its new public safety headquarters.

The statues were crafted by a sculptor in Italy and chosen by Quincy Mayor Thomas Koch.

AMERICA’S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

According to court documents, Koch said he did not pick the statues to advertise religion but to "honor, inspire and encourage our First Responders" as well as "boost morale" and "ensure [first responders’] lifesaving work would remain maximally effective."

Critics of the statues said the plan had not been publicly disclosed during the building approval process and raised constitutional concerns.

The legal battle started in May 2025, when faith groups and taxpayers sued the City of Quincy and Koch in Norfolk Superior Court, saying that the intended installation of the statues outside the city's new public safety headquarters violated the Massachusetts Constitution's protections on religious neutrality.

The plaintiffs are represented by the ACLU of Massachusetts, the national ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State, the Freedom From Religion Foundation and Cloherty & Steinberg LLP.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

The ACLU of Massachusetts wrote in its brief, "The statues, whose imagery is drawn directly from Catholic iconography, lack a predominantly secular purpose. The primary effect of permanently installing two new, oversized, overtly religious statues as the sole adornments on the City’s public safety building is to advance religion."

The National Fraternal Order of Police and Massachusetts Fraternal Order of Police, however, said in a brief that St. Michael is revered by people of various faiths, not just Christians.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

"First responders of all stripes, religious creeds, and political affiliations — and not just Catholics or Christians — cherish both saints for their symbolic importance to the profession," the brief states.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Koch, the mayor of Quincy, said, "Quincy’s firefighters and police put their lives on the line for this city every day, and these statues were chosen to honor their bravery, service, and sacrifice."

Koch added, "This decision is disappointing, but it is preliminary, and we will continue to fight for the ability to commemorate our first responders as the law permits."

In a statement, Jessie Rossman, legal director at the ACLU of Massachusetts, said, "Here in Massachusetts, our state constitution is clear: the government must remain neutral in matters of religion and must not elevate one faith above others. With today's landmark ruling, the Supreme Judicial Court affirms those principles, which are the essential foundation of a pluralistic society where people of all faiths and no faith can flourish."

"As Quincy residents and taxpayers, our clients believe that installing these plainly religious statues would undermine those ideals," Rossman added. "We are proud to represent these courageous plaintiffs, and we look forward to continuing to litigate the merits of this case in Superior Court."

item.title: ‘Never give up a fight’: NYC mom shows her kids 5, 7 the scars from neck-slash attack as lesson in survival
item.description: Alexis Rowan survived a neck-slashing attack on the Havasupai Reservation after her screams drew a woman outside, and Ring camera footage captured it.
item.content:encoded:
Alexis Rowan, 27, is just a week removed from a fight for her life — stitches out, a permanent scar as the nightmare’s lasting mark — yet more resolved than ever to live as an example of strength for the children she begged to come home to.

It was the fight over flight she learned from her mother, Tricia Rowan, a self-described descendant of boxing legacy.

"Get your daughter in MMA," Tricia Rowan, told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday. "That's what I'm signing my grandkids up for this fall."

NYC MOM SURVIVES NECK-SLASH ATTACK ON HIKING TRIP IN ARIZONA: 'I CAN’T DIE LIKE THIS'

Her daughter, Alexis, survived a death-defying, neck-slashing attack Wednesday, Aug. 19, in northern Arizona's Havasupai Indian Reservation, and they are using the moment to warn women, Americans, and even their kids/grandkids (5 and 7) of what "literal screaming for your life is; that is what fighting for your life" truly sounds like.

"She is a true example of what it means to make the noise so someone comes to your rescue," Tricia Rowan said. "Never just take anything laying down, like scream, fight and she did it. She's a warrior."

WITNESSES RECOUNT 'SCARY' NYC STABBING AFTER SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY YELLED 'ALLAHU AKBAR' DURING ATTACKS

Alexis Rowan admitted she needed nearly a week to rehear and rewatch the attack recorded on a nearby Ring camera, but she is resolute in using the moment now and not shielding her young children from the scars left by the shocking Arizona hiking-trail attack that nearly took her life.

"It's, you know, right there – and especially before like I had all the stitches in it," Alexis Rowan said. "So, of course, they look at me and it's the first thing they see."

THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN

"I like my kids to be aware like just like I was always raised: You have to be aware of your surroundings; I'm not going to sit and lie to them because things like this does happen in life.

"You see it on the news, you see anything, 'oh my God, that can never happen.' No, it could happen, so I always tell my kids: You have to pay attention.

JO FROST CALLS OUT MODERN PARENTING MISTAKES SHE SAYS ARE ROBBING CHILDREN OF BASIC LIFE SKILLS

"Living in New York City, always be aware, like pay attention from everywhere. Just be aware.

"Even though, yes, they are little," she continued, "but they need to be aware that things like this can happen.

"You can't panic. We have to think smart, make a decision... be aware."

FBI HEADQUARTERS WELCOMES UFC FIGHTERS FOR TRAINING SESSIONS AHEAD OF HISTORIC WHITE HOUSE MMA EVENT

The 27-year-old New York City mother was hiking through the Havasupai Reservation when she said a man came up behind her and slashed her neck after she asked him for directions to a gift shop.

Her fight versus flight sensed something was "not right."

The man, following her at a distance, led her to call home because she was afraid, telling the person on the line that she was not safe when he asked if she was.

ALASKA RUNNER HOSPITALIZED AFTER USING BEAR SPRAY TO FIGHT OFF BROWN BEAR ON ALASKA TRAIL

"As soon as I said, 'No,' the man came behind me and sliced my own neck," Rowan said, sharing a photo that showed the deep gash in her neck as Ring camera footage showed the blood flowing over her and her 60 pounds of hiking gear.

The attack became a blur, she said, as she feared she was bleeding to death.

"I was like, ‘I’m going to die. Like, I can’t die like this. Like, I have my kids to go home to. Like, they need me,’" Alexis Rowan recalled. "This is not the way I’m gonna die.

"All of these thoughts are like running through my head."

SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY SPAT ON WOMAN BEFORE TACKLING HER IN LATE-NIGHT STORE ATTACK NEAR UPENN CAMPUS

A woman from the nearby gift shop came outside after hearing the commotion, Ring camera footage obtained by Fox News Digital showed, frightening off the attacker and ushering her into the home to wait for help.

The Rowans called the woman who saved her life a hero. That woman in the gift shop wanted to remain anonymous. She personally knew the reservation member, and knew he was a dangerous man with an alleged history of preying on women in the reservation, perhaps why she initially came out of the door before briefly retreating.

Tricia Rowan said the instinct to fight had long been a central lesson in their family.

"It’s always about self-protection, self-awareness and never go down without a fight — whatever it takes — and always scream," she said. "I was so proud of the warrior that she was for screaming for her life."

‘HERO' MOM DIES AFTER USING LAST STRENGTH TO SAVE 4-YEAR-OLD SON FROM FLORIDA RIVER

The family said the scream that drew the woman outside was the difference between life and death. Tricia Rowan initially hesitated to release Ring camera footage with sound that captured her daughter’s cries, concerned about the trauma it could cause Alexis and her grandchildren. But she said she now believes the public needs to hear it.

"People got so numb to violence," Tricia Rowan said. "Until you hear that video of my daughter, that is what literal screaming for your life is. That is what fighting for your life is."

She said, Alexis, despite carrying heavy camping bags and suffering the sudden attack, "is a true example" of why people in danger should "make the noise so someone comes to your rescue."

The Rowans said their family has a history of resilience, including a line of strong women who raised children through adversity. Tricia Rowan said she also learned that a distant relative, John L. Sullivan, was a famed boxer — a fitting connection, she said, for a family now focused on teaching the next generation to defend themselves.

"Never give up a fight," Tricia Rowan said. "Just fight for everything that you think is right."

item.title: Wounded Marines relive the harrowing Kabul airport attack in explosive new Fox Nation documentary
item.description: Tyler Vargas-Andrews and other retired U.S. Marines recount the Abbey Gate bombing at Kabul's international airport in a Fox Nation documentary tracing mistakes behind the attack.
item.content:encoded:
Five years after the deadly explosion at Kabul International Airport in Afghanistan, Fox Nation takes an exclusive look at the harrowing incident and the ramifications it had on the U.S. military and American foreign policy.

"Ambush at Abbey Gate: The Afghanistan Withdrawal," a new 40-minute documentary, aims to uncover the mistakes made that led to the suicide bombing at Abbey Gate, a major entrance to Hamid Karzai International Airport.

Retired U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Tyler Vargas-Andrews, who lost his right and left leg in the explosion, spoke out about the terrifying experience with the show's host, Joey Jones.

GOLD STAR FATHER SAYS PRIOR AFGHANISTAN REVIEW SMELLED 'LIKE A COVER-UP' AS NEW LOOK EXAMINES MILLIONS OF DOCS

"Staff Sergeant Darren 'Taylor' Hoover was killed next to me," he said. "My whole abdomen, you know, had been ripped open. I took 150 ball bearings into my body, lost my left kidney. I lost 157 centimeters, large and small intestine."

Retired U.S. Marine Corps Cpl. Kelsee Lainhart was also hurt in the surprise attack, describing the ordeal as damaging several different parts of her body.

DOLLY PARTON'S ‘ALL-AMERICAN HEART’: HOW COUNTRY ICON FORGED SPECIAL BOND WITH US MILITARY

"Different shrapnel and ball bearings hit me in the blast," she said. "I have a ball bearing in my skull, a few other parts of my body, and then the shrapnel hit my vertebrae."

The incident killed 11 Marines, one sailor and one soldier on that fateful day in August 2021. Among the dead were 45 injured American service members, many with severe injuries. More than 160 Afghan civilians were also killed in the blast.

Vargas-Andrews vowed he and his fellow soldiers impacted by the Kabul attack would never let the memory of the day fade away. 

"We'll never be forgotten," he said. "[This] mentally wounded the entirety of the 'GWOT' [Global War on Terrorism] generation."

The documentary traces not only the Kabul attack itself, but also the injured soldiers' inspirations for joining the U.S. military, despite many criticizing the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan as an "absolute disaster," Jones said.

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

"I remember going up to my mom's room, and I was, like, 'Hey, I'm going to join the Marine Corps.'" Vargas-Andrews said. "I knew it was a place that I could hopefully go and become a man and help those less fortunate. And still to this day, enlisting in the Marine Corps is the best decision I've ever made in my life."

Former Army aviator Rep. Matt Van Epps, R-Tenn., recently blasted the Biden administration over the controversial U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

"The Biden-Harris administration absolutely failed to withdraw from Afghanistan, and it didn't have to be that way," Van Epps told Fox News Digital. "And it's important for the American people to remember what the Biden-Harris administration did in that abject failure, withdrawing from Afghanistan." 

The congressman also introduced a resolution marking the fifth anniversary of the shocking bombing at Hamid Karzai International Airport.

To uncover more about the somber legacy of the Kabul bombing and America's tumultuous exit from Afghanistan, tune into "Ambush at Abbey Gate: The Afghanistan Withdrawal," now streaming on Fox Nation.

item.title: Commanders' Jayden Daniels deflects question on LSU cease-and-desist letter after social media trolling wave
item.description: Jayden Daniels deflected questions about his LSU cease-and-desist letter after the New York Mets, StubHub, and thousands trolled him on social media.
item.content:encoded:
Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels’ cease-and-desist letter to LSU earlier this month over the use of his name, image and likeness completely backfired – at least in the eyes of football fans.

Daniels was taking a stand after what he viewed as a "disrespectful" move allowing current Tigers cornerback DJ Pickett to wear his No. 5, the number he wore at LSU, heading into the 2026 college season.

What transpired after releasing a statement on Instagram about why he filed the cease-and-desist letter against LSU ultimately backfired into a tsunami of social media trolling.

JAYDEN DANIELS WANTED ‘RESPECT’ FROM LSU. INSTEAD, HE STARTED AN UGLY FIGHT THAT WILL TARNISH HIS REPUTATION

The New York Mets, StubHub, Columbia’s football social page, and many more trolled Daniels with their own version of "respect" for the dual-threat quarterback. The Mets posted a final score of a victory against the Washington Nationals, which finished 4-1, saying, "Stopped at 4 out of respect for Jayden Daniels."

For StubHub, the ticket marketplace jokingly posted "we will no longer offer tickets in groups of 5. Out of respect for Jayden Daniels…"

Thousands of other social media users did the same, and Daniels himself hadn’t spoken to the media to give his reaction. At the end of his press conference on Wednesday following a joint practice against the Baltimore Ravens, Daniels’ final question was about the cease-and-desist letter and whether he had anything else to say.

"I posted the statement on Instagram and said everything I needed to say. So, appreciate y’all," Daniels replied, deflecting any sort of additional comment on the matter.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The move has simply blown up in his face and created a whirlwind of finger-pointing and trolling on social media. But while it’s not ideal heading into a season with that sort of distraction on the outside, Daniels has appeared calm and collected as he prepares for a new year.

Daniels noted being "locked in on training camp" in his statement regarding the cease-and-desist letter to LSU. But he still feels slighted by his former team that he won a Heisman Trophy with before heading to the NFL.

"I have been locked in on training camp and that's been my number one focus. I have a lot of gratitude for my time at LSU and I'm proud of what my teammates and I accomplished there," Daniels posted. "Obviously there are issues to be worked out between my team and LSU and my hope is that it will get done privately.

"My sole personal focus is on Commanders' football. I realize the business of football is unique and I trust this can all be resolved."

Daniels is hoping that him and his No. 5 Commanders jersey is on the field for the entirety of the 2026 NFL season after injuries took a toll in his sophomore campaign.

Daniels was the Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2024, leading the Commanders to the NFC Championship Game in shocking fashion after defeating the Detroit Lions on the road in the Divisional Round. But he only participated in seven games last year as the Commanders were unable to make it back to the playoffs.

item.title: Tap-to-pay charity scam can cost you thousands
item.description: A tap-to-pay charity scam is turning small $15 or $20 donations into charges of nearly $5,000, with victims losing thousands before they notice.
item.content:encoded:
Tap to pay has become one of my favorite modern conveniences. I use it all the time. In fact, I rarely need to pull out a physical wallet anymore because contactless payments are accepted in so many places.

There's a security advantage, too. Mobile wallets can use tokenization or virtual card numbers, so your actual card number does not need to pass directly to a merchant during a transaction.

That makes what's happening with a tap-to-pay charity scam especially frustrating. Criminals are taking a technology designed to make paying easier and using a moment of distraction to turn a small donation into a potentially massive charge.

You may think you're giving $5 or $20 to a good cause. Then you check your account and discover hundreds or even thousands of dollars are gone. Here's how the scam works and what you can do to protect your money.

APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES

New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

The setup can feel completely ordinary. You're leaving a store, walking through a busy shopping area or heading through a public event. Someone approaches you and claims to be raising money for a youth group, school fundraiser or another cause. They ask for a small donation. Maybe you agree to $5. Maybe you offer $20. Then they tell you they can accept tap to pay. That's when you need to pay very close attention.

One version of the scam involves the solicitor entering a much larger amount into a smartphone or payment reader before you tap your phone or card. You think you're approving $20. The payment screen may actually say $2,000. If you tap without carefully checking that amount, you could authorize the larger transaction. Brentwood police warned in January 2026 about a version involving people approaching shoppers outside stores for small donations. Police said victims could be charged significantly more than expected after using tap to pay, Square or Cash App.

The numbers can get ugly fast. The Washington state attorney general issued a warning after receiving reports involving solicitors near the Seattle waterfront. In one case, a person agreed to donate $15 and later discovered a $4,800 charge. Another person agreed to give $20 and later found a charge of nearly $5,000. Those examples show why you should never treat the final tap as a formality.

There's another risk worth keeping in mind. If someone claims the transaction failed and asks to take your phone to help, end the transaction. A scammer does not need to take your phone for the inflated-payment scheme to work. However, handing over an unlocked phone creates a much bigger security problem. Depending on your settings, that person may be able to reach email, messages, payment apps or financial information. I would never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger during any financial transaction.

Tap to pay itself remains a secure way to make legitimate purchases. The weakness here involves what you approve. If a scammer puts $2,000 on the payment screen and you authenticate that transaction, the payment system sees an approved purchase.

The criminal is counting on you to skip one very important step: reading the amount before tapping. We use contactless payments so frequently that the gesture can become automatic. Pull out the phone. Authenticate. Tap. Walk away. That routine gives a scammer an opening.

CyberGuy has previously covered how quickly mobile payment scams can turn into serious financial losses through services such as Venmo, Zelle and Cash App.

You do not need to stop using tap-to-pay. I certainly don't plan to. Instead, change how you handle unexpected payment requests.

Never give a stranger your unlocked phone to complete or troubleshoot a payment. If something supposedly went wrong with a transaction, cancel it and move on. When your financial information is involved, you should stay in control of your device from beginning to end.

This may be the single most important habit. Stop for a second and look at the amount displayed on the merchant's phone or payment terminal. Do this before your phone or card goes anywhere near the reader. If you agreed to donate $10, make sure the screen says $10. The FTC also recommends reviewing your financial statements after making donations to confirm you were charged only the amount you intended.

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

A legitimate cause will still exist five minutes from now. If someone tells you that you need to donate immediately, I would walk away. Scammers often rely on pressure because they do not want you thinking too carefully about the request. The FTC specifically advises people against letting fundraisers rush them into making a donation.

Ask for the organization's name, then look it up independently. Do not rely on a website, QR code or social media account the solicitor hands you. Search for the charity yourself and check whether it is registered. Look for independent reviews and see how the organization says donations should be made. The FTC recommends researching unfamiliar charities before sending money.

If the cause sounds worthwhile, you can still donate. Go directly to the organization's official website after you have verified it. That gives you time to confirm who will receive your money without someone standing over you waiting for a tap.

I'm a big fan of account alerts because they can tell you the moment something happens with your money. Turn on notifications for card purchases and withdrawals. Also, consider alerts for transfers or other significant account activity. If you intended to donate $20 and immediately get an alert showing $2,000, you can contact your financial institution right away.

Check the security settings inside apps such as Venmo, Cash App, PayPal and your bank's mobile app. Enable Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a separate PIN when the app offers those protections. That creates another barrier if someone ever gets access to your unlocked phone.

If you spot an inflated charge or realize you approved far more than you intended, move quickly. The sooner you respond, the sooner your bank can tell you what options are available.

Call the bank or card issuer connected to the transaction. Explain exactly what happened. Tell them how much you agreed to pay and how much was actually charged. Ask whether the transaction can be stopped, disputed or reversed. If your banking app allows it, consider locking the affected card while you investigate. Brentwood police specifically advise suspected victims of this scam to contact their bank or card issuer immediately.

Take screenshots of the transaction and save any payment confirmations. Write down where the encounter happened and approximately what time it occurred. Also record the merchant name shown with the charge. Those details can help your bank or law enforcement investigate.

If the scammer ever handled your unlocked phone, review the financial apps installed on it. Look for unfamiliar transfers or purchases. Then check whether anyone changed your email address, phone number or other account information. Continue watching those accounts over the following days because suspicious activity may appear later.

If a stranger had access to your unlocked device, change passwords for sensitive accounts that may have been exposed. I would start with your primary email account because criminals can use email to reset passwords elsewhere. Then secure banking and payment accounts. Use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available.

HOW FLORIDA RETIREE LOST $200K IN FAKE PAYPAL REFUND SCAM

Make sure your phone requires Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a strong passcode. Also protect sensitive apps when your device offers that option. The goal is to keep someone from turning a few seconds with your unlocked phone into access to your financial life.

Antivirus software will not reverse an inflated tap-to-pay transaction. However, it becomes much more relevant if the scammer convinced you to click a link, visit a website or download something. Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious software and warn you about dangerous links used in follow-up scams. I recommend running trusted security protection across your devices and keeping it updated. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Fraudsters often come back for a second attempt. If they learn your name, phone number or other personal details, they can combine that information with data already available online to make the next scam more convincing. Data brokers and people-search sites can expose personal information about you. You can remove much of this information yourself. However, the process can take time and information may reappear. A data removal service can automate many of those removal requests and continue checking for your information. It cannot erase information a criminal already obtained. Still, reducing your online footprint gives scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

If someone gained access to sensitive information on your phone, you may want an additional set of eyes watching for signs of fraud. Identity theft protection services can monitor for suspicious activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places it should not. Some services also provide recovery assistance if your identity gets misused. That can be especially useful if you believe the incident exposed more than a payment card. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

A fraudulent tap-to-pay charge by itself does not automatically mean someone can open credit in your name. However, the situation changes if a scammer also obtained sensitive personal information that could be used for identity theft. In that case, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new credit account in your name.

If you lost money, report what happened. Contact local law enforcement when appropriate, especially if the amount is significant or the same solicitors appear to be targeting other people. You can also report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If the person claimed to represent a charity, consider contacting your state attorney general or charity regulator as well.

I still like mobile wallets and I still plan to use tap to pay. The technology gives us convenience along with useful payment protections.

What changes for me is how I handle a stranger asking for a quick donation. I want to know exactly who is getting my money before I approve anything.

If I decide the cause deserves support, I can look up the organization later and donate directly through its verified website. That approach removes the pressure and gives me time to make sure my money reaches the people I intended to help.

Tap to pay remains one of my favorite ways to check out. I like the speed and I like the added security mobile wallets can provide. Still, technology cannot protect you from every number you personally approve. That's what makes this scam effective. Most of us have become so comfortable tapping that we barely think about the final transaction screen. I want that habit to change. Before you tap, look at the amount. If a stranger is asking for a donation, give yourself time to verify the organization first. And if anyone asks to take your unlocked phone during the process, my answer would be an immediate no. Your generosity should reach the cause you chose, rather than a scammer counting on a few distracted seconds.

Would you still tap your phone to donate to someone who approached you in public after seeing how easily a small gift can become a four-figure charge? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Female Little Leaguer is smashing records, CBS's new college football reporter & heartbreaking sports moments!
item.description: Kinley Rasmus set the LLWS record for most hits by a girl while her dad Cory Rasmus and uncle Colby Rasmus both played in MLB as pros.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Hump Day of August. Seriously. Weren't we just doing this in July? And now, we're six days away from September.

Lordy. Be careful. You blink, and it'll be Halloween. Blink again, and we'll be rocking around the Christmas tree. Summer goes by faster and faster each year, doesn't it?

As you get older, you really do understand what your grandparents meant when they said "it goes by faster each year." My grandma used to say that all the time. I rolled my eyes. Not anymore.

We're 72 hours away from kickoff in Dublin. Red Sox-Yanks this weekend in the Bronx for what is essentially a playoff series to decide who hosts who in October. I'll be in Daytona for the Firecracker 400.

item.title: Judge clears path for ICE agent accused in Minnesota shooting case to leave Texas jail
item.description: A federal judge denied Minnesota's temporary restraining order, potentially clearing ICE agent Christian Castro's release from Cameron County Jail.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge on Wednesday handed Minnesota a major setback in its fight to keep ICE agent Christian Castro behind bars in Texas, denying an emergency request that would have blocked his release Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. rejected Minnesota’s request for a temporary restraining order barring Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino from releasing Castro while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott decides whether to extradite the agent to face assault charges.

Castro’s 90-day detention period under Texas law expires Thursday. Trevino’s counsel told the court that without a court order or a rendition warrant signed by Abbott, Castro would be released from the Cameron County Jail.

Rodriguez wrote that Minnesota "fails to satisfy the requirements for the issuance of a temporary restraining order."

'POLITICAL STUNT' PROSECUTION OF ICE AGENT FOR 'ROAD RAGE' PROVOKES HEATED DHS RESPONSE

Minnesota had asked the court to force Abbott to immediately issue a rendition warrant and prevent Castro’s release in the meantime. The state warned Castro could flee to Mexico, pointing to jail calls with a woman described in court filings as his romantic partner who lives in Progreso, Mexico.

According to the order, Castro discussed buying property and moving to Mexico in the future. Minnesota argued that if he left the country, it could take months or years to secure his return and prosecute him.

But Rodriguez ruled that Minnesota’s lawsuit was premature because Abbott has not yet denied its extradition request.

"The record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro," the judge wrote.

Abbott instead directed the Texas secretary of state to investigate whether Castro should be surrendered, a step permitted under Texas’ Uniform Criminal Extradition Act. Rodriguez found that neither the Constitution nor state and federal extradition laws at issue impose a set deadline for Abbott to complete that review.

"The Court concludes that this matter does not present an issue ripe for adjudication," Rodriguez wrote.

Minnesota formally requested Castro’s extradition in early June, after he was arrested in Cameron County on the state’s warrant. The court noted Abbott has considered the matter for an "atypically-long duration," but said Minnesota identified no law requiring the governor to act within a particular time frame.

TIM WALZ PARDONS ILLEGAL ALIEN CONVICTED OF ARMED ROBBERY BEFORE ICE DEPORTATION TO LAOS

Castro was charged in May with four felony counts of second-degree assault and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime stemming from a January ICE operation in Minnesota.

According to the order, Castro fired one shot through the closed front door of a home, injuring a person in the leg. 

The shooting sparked protests in north Minneapolis and has become part of a broader political and legal battle between Minnesota officials and the Trump administration over state prosecutions of ICE agents who took part in Operation Metro Surge.

15 ANTIFA RADICALS INDICTED, 12 ARRESTED IN SWEEPING FEDERAL PROBE INTO MINNEAPOLIS ANTI-ICE OPERATIONS

Minnesota prosecutors have separately charged ICE agent Gregory Morgan Jr. with two counts of second-degree assault after alleging he pointed a handgun at motorists during a traffic confrontation after an enforcement operation.

DHS has accused Minnesota "sanctuary politicians" of staging a "political stunt," while Minnesota officials have argued the agents’ alleged conduct fell outside their federal law-enforcement duties.

Abbott has raised questions about whether Castro can be considered a fugitive for extradition purposes because he returned to Texas on orders from federal immigration officials after the January incident.

Rodriguez, however, signaled skepticism of that reasoning in a footnote.

"The Court has doubts that caselaw supports the construction of ‘fugitive’ that Texas is considering," he wrote, noting that long-standing precedent appears to focus on whether an accused person left the state — not why.

Still, the judge said that question did not alter Wednesday’s decision.

The ruling leaves Castro’s immediate fate in Abbott’s hands. If no rendition warrant is issued and no court order intervenes, he is expected to be released Thursday.

Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Fox News' Patrick McGovern and Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

item.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Social media addiction will easily outlast Meta's massive multibillion-dollar settlement
item.description: Meta's proposed $17 billion social media settlement may actually benefit the company, given potential penalties that were estimated at $1.4 trillion.
item.content:encoded:
It is not every day that a company can settle a case for over $17 billion and celebrate. However, Meta’s proposed settlement of claims brought by a coalition originally led by 29 states on Wednesday is a remarkably good deal for a company facing potential penalties that Meta estimated could reach $1.4 trillion and years of litigation. In the end, the company may not even take a loss from the litigation.

The proposed settlement ends the states’ federal case (but not the wider wave of litigation), following similar settlements in tobacco, opiates and other products. It will require Meta to make changes to its platform, though the company has already appeared to be moving to make such changes.

The maximum payment of closer to $17.1 billion is tied to whether other social media companies, TikTok and YouTube, for example, adopt parallel protections for children. Otherwise, the company is on the hook for at least $12.1 billion over 10 years under the agreement.

META SETTLES FEDERAL TRIAL OVER CLAIMS FACEBOOK, INSTAGRAM ADDICT CHILDREN

The company agreed to proposed settlement terms that would impose daily time limits for underage users, "nighttime blocks" from midnight to 6 a.m., and notifications linked to school hours.

It is doubtful that these "fixes" will actually fix the problem. Social media is enormously popular with adults and children alike. It is also ubiquitous and accessible, particularly for tech-savvy kids. The burden will remain with parents regarding access to and use of social media, not the company.

Meta was looking at a long slog in the courts. Some of us were skeptical of the legal basis for some of these claims. The line between a popular and an "addictive" product is fairly subjective. It was hard to see where the line would have been drawn in this litigation. However, Meta likely would have faced similar demands for changes to its platforms through legislation even if it prevailed in litigation.

Those legal questions will now have to wait for another test case. The settlement leaves other companies in a more exposed position. This massive settlement is like a dinner gong for plaintiff's lawyers who will now fan out in packs in pursuit of companies like dusk on the Serengeti. Companies are already facing thousands of such lawsuits.

FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15

Meta has suffered adverse rulings in California and New Mexico, though the cases involved different claims and are subject to further appellate proceedings.

It’s clear that the company’s priority was to limit the potential damages rather than to make new law.

The actual damages are not as daunting as it may seem. The tobacco multistate settlement was over $206 billion, not counting separate state settlements worth tens of millions more. The opiate settlements resulted in damages of roughly $60 billion.

Even at more than potentially $17 billion, for a company the size of Meta, this is like monopoly money (literally so, if you ask some critics). The value of settling the case alone could potentially wipe out that loss through stock-market gains and other pricing changes. After the tobacco settlement, companies like Philip Morris enjoyed market gains that effectively washed out the loss. Moreover, these companies enjoyed a very inelastic market, so they internalized costs with price hikes that left smokers holding the bag.

Ironically, if social media is as addictive as claimed by litigants, the market is equally inelastic. Big media will be able to easily recoup these damages, as did Big Tobacco. Much of these damages could ultimately be passed on to and borne by social media users through advertising, production or cost decisions. They would potentially operate like a tax for states receiving the funds.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

The platform will clearly make positive changes that will assist parents after Wednesday’s proposed settlement announcement. These are straightforward changes that have long been needed. Hopefully, these states will not just take this money and run as many did with the tobacco windfall. Instead, it would be a great help if the money went to enhancing children’s mental-health programs.

Social media remains one of the most transformative inventions in history, including as a powerful tool for free speech and political discourse. That popularity comes at a price. It will remain part of our social fabric, as are alcohol and tobacco products despite their abuse.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Meta did not create these social costs alone. We all did. We find ourselves overwhelmed by a technology with endless applications and potential for expression. This settlement will not erase those social costs any more than the tobacco settlement erased cancer or the opiate settlement erased addiction.

The ultimate child-protection regulation will remain parents monitoring and educating their own children.

Meta's internal credo, "Meta, Metamates, and Me," may capture the problem. It is often hard for people to separate themselves from their virtual selves. This is a technology that is both liberating and captivating.

Ultimately, despite the progress under this agreement, no settlement will protect us from ourselves.

item.title: America’s heartland comes face-to-face with 9/11 history as 25th anniversary nears
item.description: The Steel Across America tour brought a 16,900-pound South Tower beam to Cincinnati and Scott Nokes, a double amputee veteran, shared his story.
item.content:encoded:
A nearly 17,000-pound piece of steel from the World Trade Center’s South Tower made its way to Cincinnati, giving people hundreds of miles from Ground Zero a rare chance to stand face-to-face with a piece of 9/11 history.

"Never forgetting the sacrifice and bravery of our nation’s heroes, as well as our lost loved ones, is a generational promise that every American can help keep," Tunnel to Towers Foundation Chairman and CEO Frank Siller told Fox News Digital.

The 21-foot steel beam is making its way across the country as part of Tunnel to Towers’ Steel Across America tour, a traveling memorial marking 25 years since the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

Former Marine infantryman Scott Nokes, a Tunnel to Towers ambassador and employee, joined local firefighters, FDNY members, veterans, first responders and community members in bringing the beam to the Cincinnati Fire Museum Saturday.

TUNNEL TO TOWERS ANNOUNCES STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR TO MARK 25 YEARS SINCE 9/11 ATTACKS

"I know firsthand what it means to have the Tunnel to Towers Foundation show up for you when you need it most," Nokes said at the event.

"This foundation changes lives. It changed mine. When I stand before this steel and think about the men and women we lost on September 11, I feel an obligation to make sure their story keeps being told. I am honored to be here today as part of this journey."

MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA

New Jersey native Nokes was deployed twice to Afghanistan before leaving the service to pursue firefighting. In 2016, he went into septic shock, and life-saving treatment left him a double below-the-knee amputee and legally blind.

Through Tunnel to Towers’ Smart Home Program, Nokes received a custom, mortgage-free smart home in December 2019 designed to help him live more independently. In addition to working and representing T2T, Nokes mentors for Neptune Emergency Services.

The stop gave community members, first responders, veterans and residents a chance to see the artifact in person during a ceremony featuring a color guard, bagpipes, the national anthem, a blessing of the beam, a moment of silence, remarks from fire and city leaders and a steel flag presentation.

AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET

The steel beam has served as a traveling memorial to the victims and first responders of 9/11, offering pop-up events across 21 different states leading up to the anniversary of the tragic day.

After Cincinnati, the tour heads into its final stretch, with stops scheduled at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point on Sept. 1, the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial in Boston Sept. 3 and the White House on Sept. 8 before returning to New York City.

The foundation provides mortgage-free, fully accessible smart homes for catastrophically injured U.S. veterans and first responders.

The foundation is honoring the 343 FDNY firefighters who died on 9/11 by delivering 343 mortgage-free homes this year.

item.title: 2028 Dem hopeful slaps Trump administration with lawsuit over mail-in voting after major SCOTUS victory
item.description: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined 23 states to sue the USPS over Trump-backed mail-ballot rule, arguing Congress — not the president or Postal Service — sets federal election rules.
item.content:encoded:
With the November midterms approaching, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is joining attorneys general from 23 states and Washington, D.C., in suing the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) over a Trump-backed mail-in ballot rule that would impose new federal requirements on how states prepare and send mail ballots.

"I’m suing the Trump Administration to stop their unconstitutional attempt to change the rules and restrict mail-in voting. I’ll remind the President of my track record going up against him in court — and winning — to protect Pennsylvania’s free, fair, safe, and secure elections. I’m prepared to do so again," Shapiro wrote on X. "Nothing about voting by mail has changed here in Pennsylvania. You can still vote safely and securely by mail.

"While Donald Trump may try to inject chaos into our elections, the Constitution is clear: the authority to set election rules belongs to the states — not the federal government."

The two-dozen state coalition returned to court two days after the Supreme Court stayed an earlier injunction issued by a Massachusetts federal judge against key parts of Trump’s mail-voting executive order, finding the states’ initial challenge premature because USPS had not yet issued a final rule when they filed suit.

TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"The Supreme Court ruling was a major win for the security of American elections. Radical Democrats continue to oppose commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. 

"The Trump administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on, which includes the safety and security of our elections."

At issue is USPS’s newly finalized "Ballot Mail for Federal Elections" rule, which went into effect last week and was published Wednesday. 

It would require state and local election officials to submit information on intended mail-in ballot recipients to a USPS portal, where the agency would compile state-specific lists of enrolled mail voters. It would also require certain mail-in ballot design requirements, such as trackable barcodes, and require officials to submit ballot-envelope designs to USPS for pre-approval.

In their 53-page complaint, the states argue that the rule improperly gives USPS a new role in running elections, forcing election officials to adopt new procedures, share ballot recipient information and potentially replace already-purchased envelopes as the midterms draw closer. 

They also argue that Congress, not the president or Postal Service, has the authority to alter election rules and that USPS skipped a review process for major nationwide changes to postal services or operations.

NEWSOM PROMISES NEW LEGAL FIGHT AFTER TRUMP GETS SUPREME COURT VICTORY ON MAIL-IN VOTING

The coalition is asking the court to block the rule while the lawsuit proceeds and ultimately throw it out, arguing that their new challenge answers the Supreme Court’s timing concern. A separate Massachusetts injunction had temporarily blocked the USPS from putting the requirements in place for the November midterms, but the judge lifted that order Wednesday after the Supreme Court’s ruling.

"This Court held that 'no law enacted by Congress delegates authority to control mail-in voting to USPS,' and that the President’s directives to USPS were ultra vires," the states wrote in their complaint. 

"The Supreme Court subsequently stayed the injunction — not because Plaintiff States’ claims lacked merit, but because the States 'lack[ed] standing to bring' their claims as to the [Executive Order].

"As the Court explained, USPS had not yet implemented the EO, but if USPS ultimately adopts a final rule that 'harms the States, they may challenge that rule.' USPS then published its final rule two days later."

The USPS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication.

item.title: Hundreds of volunteers pull 360-tonne historic Japanese castle back into place by hand
item.description: About 1,800 volunteers pulled ropes to move the 360-tonne Hirosaki Castle keep back into position using hikiya, an ancient Japanese moving technique.
item.content:encoded:
Japan enlisted the help of hundreds of volunteers to move a portion of a 360-tonne castle more than six feet back into position, inch by inch, following renovations to the structure.

About 1,800 people gathered over the weekend to pull large ropes attached to the Hirosaki Castle keep in Aomori Prefecture, The Independent reported.

The keep — which is a fortified tower within a castle — was moved so repairs could be completed on a wall damaged during a major earthquake. The wall has since been rebuilt, with all 2,185 stones returned to their original positions.

JAPAN MALL REBUILT AFTER DEADLY 2016 EARTHQUAKE DESTROYED IN MAJOR TEMBLOR WEEKS AFTER 'FRESH START' REOPENING

Rotating teams used an ancient technique known as hikiya, in which buildings are placed on rollers or rails and moved intact. The technique is used to preserve historic Japanese buildings that might otherwise be damaged or destroyed.

"We had about 8,000 applications for the 1,800 slots over the last two days, roughly four times oversubscribed, so not everyone could participate," Kensuke Hayasaka, head of the parks and green spaces division in Hirosaki City, told The Guardian.

"Not only from the city, but from across Japan and overseas; a fair number from Southeast Asia, Europe and North America."

MASSIVE 7.7-MAGNITUDE EARTHQUAKE HITS OFF JAPANESE COAST

Pulling the castle keep by hand will continue through the end of August, with about 4,100 people scheduled to move it a total of more than 16 feet, The Guardian reported.

The Hirosaki Castle keep was originally a five-story tower, but it was destroyed by a lightning strike in 1627, the newspaper reported, citing the Japan National Tourism Organization.

The current three-story structure was rebuilt in 1811. Many Japanese castles were dismantled after the end of the Samurai era in 1868 or were destroyed during World War II.

item.title: Dem senator turns ‘leader of the free world’ title on its head with Zelenskyy remarks
item.description: Chris Coons declared Volodymyr Zelenskyy is now the free world's primary leader, igniting fierce backlash from the White House and conservatives.
item.content:encoded:
Delaware Sen. Chris Coons is facing backlash after declaring that the United States is "no longer" the leader of the free world and pointing instead to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the national leader putting his country "on the line for freedom."

"I would say we are no longer the leaders of the free world. In fact, if anything, Volodymyr Zelenskyy is the primary national leader who is putting his country’s men and women on the line for freedom," Coons said during a town hall earlier this month.

"We need to earn our place back as leader in the free world in the future."

Coons’ remarks underscore his long-running alignment with Kyiv at a moment when President Donald Trump is pressing for an end to the war and putting a renewed emphasis on American power and national pride. 

TRUMP HAILS AMERICA AS 'MOST EXCEPTIONAL NATION EVER TO EXIST' IN MOUNT RUSHMORE SPEECH

The Delaware Democrat has been one of Congress’ more outspoken supporters of Ukraine, repeatedly backing military aid, tougher sanctions on Russia and continued U.S. engagement with Zelenskyy’s government.

Coons spoke with Dover, Delaware, Councilman Andre Boggerty alongside Rep. Sarah McBride in a virtual town hall Tuesday hosted by the Kent County Democratic Committee focused on local issues.

Coons has been a vocal advocate for sustained U.S. support for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, repeatedly pressing for military assistance and tougher sanctions on Moscow. Coons visited Kyiv in 2022 to meet with Zelenskyy and visited Odesa with Senate Foreign Relations Committee members in February to reiterate "the ironclad, bipartisan support" for Ukraine, according to a press release.

Nick Adams, special presidential envoy for American tourism, exceptionalism and values, told Fox News Digital Coons' comments are "the essence of America last."

"The United States is today, has been since 1776, and with God's grace, always will be the leader of the free world. To suggest otherwise is to ignore our Constitution and the bloodshed by our heroes who made sure that our Declaration of Independence would not just be a theoretical document but the beginning of a new era in the history of humanity," Adams said.

Adams added that no other nation can hold a candle to America, pointing to its constitutional freedoms, founding principles of liberty and belief that natural rights transcend government authority.
