item.title: Hasan Piker points the finger at AIPAC as Democrats speak out against him
item.description: Hasan Piker blamed AIPAC for the backlash against him after Democrats, including House Minorit Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Cory Booker, condemned his remarks about Jewish Americans.
item.content:encoded:
Hasan Piker's recent remarks about American Jews' support for Israel have drawn the ire of several Democratic lawmakers who have spoken out against him. The Twitch streamer has since blamed the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) for the backlash and welcomed the criticism with open arms.

"AIPAC boss call was made. they are unanimous in their hatred of me, and i welcome their hatred. if you’re a defender of israel’s genocide, of its occupation, of its child killing spree — then your boos mean nothing to me," Piker wrote in a post on X. 

He was responding to a post featuring images of statements put out by several Democrats condemning him.

ANTISEMITIC STREAMER FINALLY MAKES DEM LEADER SNAP WITH RARE REBUKE: ‘MALICIOUS’

Later, in response to a list of Democrats who had criticized him, Piker suggested that someone tabulate the total amount of money that the group had received from AIPAC, the prominent pro-Israel lobbying organization.

"We should calculate how much the aipac total is for all these candidates so we know how much the maga billionaire backed foreign govt lobby got prominent dems to keep the attention on an antizionist twitch streamer thru lies, instead of trumps admin in these critical midterms," he wrote.

Piker is no stranger to controversy, and his latest remarks have sparked a series of condemnations from Democrats.

President & CEO of Democratic Majority for Israel Brian Romick dismissed Piker's claim against AIPAC in a statement provided to Fox News Digital, calling it "a baseless conspiracy theory."

"Hasan Piker has built his brand by peddling conspiracy theories and hateful rhetoric. Rather than take responsibility for his own odious remarks, he is now promoting a baseless conspiracy theory to explain the entirely predictable backlash against him," Romick's statement said. 

"We’re pleased that so many Democratic officials have forcefully condemned his comments. Candidates who want to win should have nothing to do with him."

During a recent stream, Piker told his viewers, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews."

Several Democratic lawmakers have spoken out against Piker since he made those comments, including Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; and Hillary Scholten, D-Mich.

Rosen condemned the remarks as a "new low" for Piker, who she said had been "trafficking in antisemitic tropes for a while." She went on to say that by "blaming Jewish Americans for the violence and hate they're facing," Piker provided "an excuse to those perpetuating these anti-Jewish hate crimes."

"Let me be absolutely clear: crimes against Jews for being Jews is antisemitism plain and simple. There’s no excuse for it," she added.

SOME DEMOCRATS PRIVATELY DISGUSTED BY HASAN PIKER BUT ARE AFRAID TO PUBLICLY CRITICIZE HIM, HOUSE DEM CLAIMS

Jeffries said the claim that American Jews were "inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic."

"There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate," the House minority leader added. "We will fight the cancer of antisemitism with the fierce urgency of now."

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin also condemned Piker's remarks, saying, "Criticizing the policies and actions of the Israeli government is one thing. Blaming American Jews for the hatred, threats, and violence directed at them is something else entirely. It is dangerous, wrong, and antisemitic."

Piker's role in Democratic politics has been a hot topic among party members. Some have chosen to appear with him, while others have criticized his rhetoric. One candidate who embraced Piker during his campaign was Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

El-Sayed was widely criticized for appearing with Piker during his primary campaign against Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who he defeated. While El-Sayed has yet to offer a full-throated condemnation of Piker's rhetoric, he appeared to distance himself from the controversial streamer on Monday as the backlash against Piker unfolded.

EL-SAYED DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER DISTURBING REMARKS ABOUT JEWISH AMERICANS

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote on X.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

Piker has remained defiant amid the backlash, portraying Democratic criticism as being an AIPAC-driven campaign against him.

Fox News Digital reached out to AIPAC for comment on Piker's accusation but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Democrats condemning Hasan Piker as backlash spreads through party
item.description: Hakeem Jeffries called Hasan Piker's remarks about American Jews "dangerous and antisemitic" as top Democrats lined up to condemn the streamer.
item.content:encoded:
Prominent Democrats are lining up to condemn far-left streamer Hasan Piker after he warned that American Jews could face violence if they continue to be seen as strongly supporting Israel.

The backlash follows a stream last week in which Piker displayed an image of Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish and the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. 

Moss has said a fake audio clip is being circulated that falsely portrays him as saying he ran for Congress solely to ensure continued U.S. support for Israel.

"If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said.

PIKER DEMANDS DEMOCRATS DEFEND HIM FROM ATTACKS, CLAIMS HE’S NO ‘TOXIC RADICAL FORCE'

Piker's comments drew criticism from top Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and DNC Chair Ken Martin, as well as lawmakers who have criticized him before. Others who have appeared with Piker or defended engaging with him are now pushing back on his remarks.

Here are the Democrats speaking out:

Jeffries joined the backlash Monday, initially without mentioning Piker by name. The House Democratic leader called the claim that American Jews were inviting violence against themselves "dangerous and antisemitic."

Asked on CNN the following day whether he was referring to Piker, Jeffries said yes.

"Those comments were dangerous, malicious and antisemitic and should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square," Jeffries said.

Schneider was one of the first Democratic lawmakers to publicly take on Piker, calling him an "unapologetic antisemite" in March and warning fellow Democrats against giving a platform to people who espouse hate.

PIKER DEMANDS DEMOCRATS DEFEND HIM FROM ATTACKS, CLAIMS HE’S NO ‘TOXIC RADICAL FORCE'

Schneider renewed that criticism Tuesday, saying Piker's latest remarks were consistent with his "history of antisemitic statements."

"Hasan Piker's hateful ideas and antisemitic remarks have no place in America or our nation's politics," Schneider said.

Slotkin, who had previously criticized Piker and his involvement in Michigan Democratic politics, spoke out again after his latest comments.

"No community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views," Slotkin said, rejecting the idea that Jewish Americans should be blamed for antisemitism directed at them.

Stevens criticized Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed earlier this year for campaigning with Piker and made clear she would not do the same.

Piker was the "exact opposite" of someone she would campaign with, Stevens said. She later said she believed Piker should be condemned.

Booker's team had already kept its distance from Piker, turning down an appearance with the streamer over his past comments.

Booker went further this week, directly condemning Piker's rhetoric about Jewish Americans and saying it has no place in public discourse.

In April, McMorrow criticized Piker's role in Michigan Democratic politics and his inflammatory style.

She compared Piker's approach to that of far-right commentator Nick Fuentes, arguing that both use inflammatory rhetoric to attract attention.

Gottheimer has been among Piker's most persistent Democratic critics. In April, he joined Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York in introducing a bipartisan House resolution condemning antisemitic rhetoric from Piker and Candace Owens.

In an interview on Fox News' "America's Newsroom," Gottheimer praised Jeffries pushback against Piker, calling the streamer’s comments something "right out of the Nazi playbook," emphasizing them as "a call for violence against Jews."

Gottheimer on Tuesday also called on House leaders to bring the resolution up for a vote.

He also told CNN in an interview that anyone who does not condemn Piker’s comments is "complicit."

HASAN PIKER CALLS FOR DEMOCRATS WHO OPPOSE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO BE 'PUNISHED'

Longtime Democratic strategist James Carville drew a line between himself and part of the Democratic Party embracing Piker earlier this month.

Carville said he would leave the party if Piker's wing took control, arguing there was no room for both of them under the same political tent.

He later told Fox News' "Jesse Watters Primetime" he is not concerned about socialists taking over the Democratic Party, dismissing the party's socialist flank as a "pack of fools" and "a bunch of silly people."

Fetterman earlier this month took aim at El-Sayed over his ties to Piker during Michigan's Democratic Senate primary.

"I dare you to continue to campaign with people like Hasan Piker," Fetterman said.

Fetterman's comments were aimed primarily at Democrats associating with Piker rather than a direct response to the streamer's latest remarks.

Moskowitz distanced himself from Piker last week after defeating a Democratic primary challenger who had Piker's backing.

The Florida Democrat made clear after the race that he wanted no association with Piker or his politics.

Auchincloss rejected Piker's politics during an appearance on "Fox News Sunday," drawing a clear distinction between the streamer and the Democratic Party.

"The Democratic Party does not stand for what Hasan Piker stands for," Auchincloss said.

HASAN PIKER STANDS BY 'INTENTIONALLY PROVOCATIVE' CLAIMS THAT HAMAS IS 'A THOUSAND TIMES BETTER' THAN ISRAEL

Scholten issued one of the sharpest responses after Piker's comments about American Jews and Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss.

"Hasan Piker's talk of violence against American Jews and directly naming a Michigan elected official and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop," Scholten said Monday.

She also called Piker a "hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe" and said his rhetoric had no place in Michigan or the country.

Moss, who was directly discussed during Piker's stream, on Monday pushed back after Piker displayed his image while talking about American Jews and Israel.

Moss said there was "no room for extremism in Michigan."

Khanna's response was notable because he has appeared on Piker's show and previously defended his decision to engage with the streamer.

But on Monday, Khanna rejected Piker's latest argument, saying antisemitism should be condemned unequivocally and that Jewish people and supporters of Israel are not responsible for antisemitism directed at them.

El-Sayed, whose Michigan Senate campaign has faced criticism over his association with Piker, sought to put some distance between his campaign and the streamer after the latest controversy on Monday.

El-Sayed said Piker does not speak for him or his campaign and condemned antisemitism. He stopped short, however, of directly condemning Piker himself.

DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin joined the criticism Tuesday, bringing the national party's leadership into the dispute.

Martin condemned the idea that American Jews should be blamed for hatred, threats or violence directed at them, calling such rhetoric dangerous, wrong and antisemitic.

Rosen, co-chair of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, said Piker had used antisemitic tropes before but on Tuesday described his latest remarks as "a new low."

The Nevada Democrat rejected the suggestion that Jewish Americans bear responsibility for antisemitism or violence directed at them.

Torres, a longtime Piker critic, again spoke out Tuesday after the streamer's comments about American Jews.

The New York Democrat accused Piker of blaming Jewish victims for the antisemitism directed against them, adding to his previous criticism of the streamer.

Stanton joined the Democrats speaking out Tuesday over Piker's latest comments.

The Arizona congressman rejected the argument that Jewish Americans bear responsibility for hatred or violence directed against them.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser and Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

item.title: Millions of barrels of Iranian oil sit beyond Trump blockade as he vows ‘zero leakage’
item.description: Nearly 40 million barrels of Iranian crude sit on tankers near Malaysia, posing a test for Trump's "zero-leakage" sanctions campaign against Tehran.
item.content:encoded:
Far from the U.S. warships enforcing a blockade at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, nearly 40 million barrels of Iranian crude are sitting aboard tankers in waters near Malaysia, east of Singapore.

The cargo amounts to roughly 20 very large crude carriers’ worth of oil, a floating stockpile that could still give Tehran a way to turn crude already outside the blockade zone into cash even as the blockade sharply restricts fresh exports.

The stockpile poses a test for the Trump administration as it moves from military action and a naval blockade toward what the White House calls its financial "endgame" against Tehran.

TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN ‘SUFFOCATING’ REGIME AS OIL WELLS COULD SHUT WITHIN DAYS, BESSENT SAYS

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday launched Operation Economic Outcast, promising a "zero-leakage approach" designed to cut off Iran's remaining sources of revenue after months of pressure on its oil sales, shipping networks and financial enablers.

The blockade appears to be making it substantially harder for Iran to export new oil. China’s imports of Iranian crude have fallen to an estimated 534,000 barrels per day so far this month, down from roughly 823,000 barrels per day in July, according to provisional Kpler data reported by Reuters.

But millions of barrels that moved beyond the blockade line before it tightened remain within potential reach of buyers. Iran has an estimated 80 million barrels of crude held in floating storage, Reuters reported, with roughly half aboard vessels near Malaysia.

That leaves Washington facing a different challenge: stopping Tehran from monetizing oil the blockade did not trap.

If Iran can still turn that crude into cash, the regime can use the proceeds to pay for imports and potentially finance efforts to rebuild its military even as the blockade restricts fresh exports.

That makes the tankers near Malaysia an early test of whether the administration can deliver the "total isolation" it has promised.

CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN

"The blockade as it’s currently being practiced and enforced against isn’t really stopping the flow of Iranian oil that’s already past the blockade line," Max Meizlish, a former Treasury official focused on sanctions policy and current senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital.

Iranian oil can move through ship-to-ship transfers, in which cargo is shifted from one tanker to another at sea. The practice can help obscure the oil’s origin before it reaches a buyer, often an independent Chinese refinery.

Simply having the crude outside the blockade zone does not automatically give Tehran usable revenue. Iran still needs to deliver the oil, collect payment and move the proceeds through the financial channels it has used to evade sanctions.

Treasury has said Iran primarily settles oil sales in Chinese yuan, with exchange houses and front companies helping convert those funds into currencies the regime can use. The department has also previously tied proceeds from Iranian oil sales to the Iranian government, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, weapons development and Tehran’s regional proxies.

Meizlish noted that the administration has continued sanctioning Chinese and Hong Kong trading houses, maritime service providers and other entities accused of enabling Iranian sanctions evasion but has stopped short of designating a Chinese financial institution.

The U.S. cut the bank off from access to the American financial system in 2012 over dealings with Iran, Meizlish said, but stopped short of placing it on Treasury’s Specially Designated Nationals list. He argued that formally designating the bank could put pressure on its owner, China National Petroleum Corporation, and potentially disrupt a channel used to move Iranian oil revenue.

Meizlish noted that the administration has continued sanctioning Chinese and Hong Kong trading houses, maritime service providers and other entities accused of enabling Iranian sanctions evasion, but has so far stopped short of designating a Chinese financial institution.

"Secretary Bessent didn’t mention China by name," he said, adding that the issue could become a subject of higher-level engagement between Washington and Beijing.

The administration has already targeted the Malaysia route.

In April, Treasury sanctioned the Hong Kong-flagged tanker Lynn, saying the vessel conducted a ship-to-ship transfer of Iranian crude off Malaysia before delivering the cargo to China.

Meizlish said another option would be to expand pressure on shadow-fleet vessels operating near Malaysia and elsewhere in Asia in an effort to keep that oil from ultimately reaching Chinese buyers.

"The U.S. could expand the blockades in that sense by going after shadow fleet tankers, operating, for instance, off the coast of Malaysia, which is a huge hub for illicit ship-to-ship transfers," he said.

He said the sharp decline in Chinese purchases suggests the pressure campaign is having an effect, but argued that crude already aboard shadow-fleet tankers remains a potential future source of revenue for Tehran.

"There’s a lot more that we can do," Meizlish said.

"Unless we expect for this regime to ultimately fall, we should be putting a lot of pressure into interdicting this oil that’s on the market right now on shadow fleet tankers, because this money could eventually go into the regime’s pockets down the road," he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Asked whether the administration planned further action against Iranian oil cargoes and shadow-fleet vessels near Malaysia, a War Department official told Fox News Digital that U.S. forces would continue "global maritime enforcement" to disrupt illicit networks and interdict sanctioned vessels supporting Iran "wherever they operate, at the time and place of our choosing."

"Under Operation Economic Outcast, anyone foolish enough to continue doing business with the Iranian regime cannot continue to enjoy access to the global financial system," a Treasury Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "We will cut every remaining economic lifeline Tehran has."

Meizlish said money from oil already sitting on shadow-fleet tankers could still wind up in Tehran’s hands and help Iran rebuild military capabilities damaged in the conflict.

Going after those tankers would not be simple. The U.S. Navy is already stretched by operations in the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere, he said, and seizing ships and their cargo can trigger legal fights over ownership, custody and what happens to the oil afterward.

Meizlish said Congress could make it easier for the government to seize illicit cargoes. He also argued that Washington should look for ways to expand its capacity to pursue shadow-fleet vessels if the Navy cannot do it alone.

Bessent’s new campaign goes beyond oil, targeting digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also threatened broader secondary sanctions against entities that continue doing business with Tehran.

The drop in Chinese purchases shows Iran is having a harder time getting new oil to market. But millions of barrels are already sitting outside the blockade.

Whether Tehran can still sell that oil, and whether Washington is willing to go after it near Malaysia, will help determine how much "zero leakage" actually means.

item.title: Hot take alert: ESPN getting rid of 'BottomLine' score ticker is a travesty, not a reason to celebrate
item.description: ESPN's decision to remove the "BottomLine" score ticker from college football broadcasts is drawing praise from fans, but not everyone agrees.
item.content:encoded:
In case you missed the news, ESPN is getting rid of its "BottomLine" score ticker during college football broadcasts this coming season.

As Yahoo Sports reports, the network is trying to streamline the college football viewer experience for fans, and will remove the ticker from all broadcasts of the sport across its different channels.

ESPN has already gotten rid of the "BottomLine" during other live broadcasts such as the College Football Playoff and NBA postseason games.

As soon as I heard this news, I immediately went to social media to see what the reaction would be.

Surely, everyone felt the same way as I did, right?

That is to say, this is a horrible move by ESPN and just another way the network is taking away what we love little by little in a sort of "frog in the boiling pot of water" way.

But, much to my surprise and chagrin, the move is being widely lauded by fans across all of social media.

The vast majority of people weighing in on the removal of the "BottomLine" are doing so in support of the decision.

Some fans say it's a needless distraction, while others say they can just check their phones for the scores and call anyone who flinches at this announcement a "grandpa" or a "boomer."

THESE ONCE-ANNUAL COLLEGE RIVALRIES USED TO DEFINE COLLEGE FOOTBALL AND NEED TO MAKE A COMEBACK ASAP

If I may be so bold, these people are missing the point so badly they couldn't find it with a telescope.

This is just another example of ESPN bastardizing something that we grew up with and loved deeply: college football.

Sure, anyone can open up their phone and see that Arkansas is covering the spread against LSU, but that takes all the fun out of it.

There's nothing more electric than watching a game and seeing the ticker light up with the words "UPSET ALERT" in big, bold letters at the bottom of the screen.

Besides, who wants to be on their phones all game long anyway?

And anyone calling a ticker that takes up roughly 8% of their television screen is either being insanely disingenuous or has some serious attention span issues.

Are your brains so fried that a ticker distracts you from watching the greatest sport on earth every Saturday?

This is coming from the same people that need to have the subtitles on during their stupid Netflix documentaries, though, so it's all starting to make sense.

SEC FOOTBALL DOING AWAY WITH 'CUPCAKE WEEKEND' MEANS THE DEATH OF ANOTHER COLLEGE FOOTBALL TRADITION

Taking away the "BottomLine" ticker is just another shot in the crotch to that all-important "tradition" that makes college football king.

It will be hilarious to see these same people that are celebrating in the streets about the demise of the "BottomLine" talk about it with reverence a few decades from now.

"Man, they used to have this ticker that would tell you all the scores at the bottom of the screen. Can't believe they got rid of it."

These are also the same people that whine about ESPN doing away with the old College Football Saturday theme song and wax poetically about the scorebug from 15 years ago, so I just know they'll come around to pretending they used to care about the "BottomLine."

Enjoy your traditions while they last, kids, because Father Time comes for all of them sooner or later.

Dolly Parton’s death on Tuesday followed a brief bout with cancer, according to statements from her family.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the family shared, as confirmed by Fox News Digital.

The revelation of the singer’s previously undisclosed cancer battle raises questions about why some patients choose to keep a diagnosis private, even as public figures’ health struggles can spark wider awareness.

DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Dr. Kristin Higgins, chief clinical officer at City of Hope Cancer Center in Atlanta, surmised that Parton may have preferred people remember her for her "amazing career" and not for a diagnosis at the end of her life.

Keeping the disease private at first is a "very natural response," Higgins said, as a diagnosis can be very overwhelming.

"It's very natural to cling to that identity of being a healthy, vibrant person without a diagnosis of cancer," she told Fox News Digital.

"The patient really needs to acclimate to the idea of themselves having this disease and then start to tell friends and family kind of slowly after they go through that adjustment process."

CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

In some cases, Higgins said, people may withhold a cancer diagnosis due to some degree of shame or embarrassment.

"Things like tobacco-related cancers, unfortunately, still carry a lot of stigma when diagnosed," she shared. "Patients may feel that it was their fault. And the reality is nobody deserves a cancer diagnosis."

There are some benefits, however, to eventually sharing a cancer diagnosis with friends, family and community who can rally around the patient, according to the doctor.

"For example, for people who are religious, letting their greater circle know about that diagnosis can be really helpful, as people will pray for them as they're going through the journey of treatment," Higgins said.

"I think, overall, it's a very beneficial thing to eventually tell as many people as possible so you can get that support."

The doctor also agreed that sharing a cancer journey can raise awareness and provide support to others facing the same challenge.

"If you are somebody with a cancer diagnosis, and you're beating it, and you are going through treatment successfully, other people seeing that — whether it's on social media or hearing it through a friend — that can be really helpful to an individual as they're facing a new cancer diagnosis," Higgins said.

Another benefit of disclosing cancer is that it may open up more opportunities for treatment options.

"There are so many resources out there now. … Clinical trials are really what moved the needle in the cure rates for cancer, and finding out about these trials is not easy," Higgins noted.

"So, the more people who know about your diagnosis, you have all these cheerleaders out there rooting for you, and you can get more information. You can hear more people's opinions about where you could seek the best cancer treatment."

The doctor emphasized that there is more hope than ever for people facing a cancer diagnosis.

"Our statistic is that 70% of people diagnosed with cancer will survive five years or more," she said. "And we can do it, we can get through it.

"I think that's the beauty of sharing this diagnosis with the world is that we can get all the support we need."

item.title: CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials in visit to Moscow, Kremlin says
item.description: Video captured a C-17 Globemaster landing at Moscow's Vnukovo airport as CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly met with Russian intelligence officials.
item.content:encoded:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow to meet with Russian intelligence officials, the Kremlin reportedly said Wednesday, after video emerged of a U.S. military transport plane coming in for a landing Tuesday at Vnukovo airport.

President Donald Trump, when asked this morning about Ratcliffe’s visit on "The Glenn Beck Program," said, "He’s there on, you know, very sort of semi-routine."

"We would like to see the war with Ukraine end," Trump added, before saying, "Now something may come out of it.

"We're working very hard to get that war ended and frankly they both want to see it ended at this point."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, the CIA and the U.S. Embassy in Moscow for further comment.

US MILITARY PLANE LANDS IN MOSCOW, WITH KREMLIN CLAIMING IT HAS NO INFORMATION: REPORT

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday, according to Reuters, "All I can ⁠tell you is that there have been contacts via the security services. I can tell you that there have been no meetings with the Russian president."

The news agency cited the Kremlin as saying Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials.

"Naturally, President Putin is kept informed of everything without delay," Peskov also was quoted as saying.

The last CIA director to visit Moscow was William Burns in November 2021, three months before Russia’s war against Ukraine started, Reuters reported.

A senior Ukrainian official told The Associated Press that Washington informed Kyiv a delegation would be traveling to the Russian capital and asked it to suspend strikes until it left.

PUTIN 'PANICKED' AS DEFIANT UKRAINE MARKS INDEPENDENCE DAY UNDER RUSSIAN BOMBARDMENT

The official said the request did not apply to all Russian territory, but specifically to Moscow, St. Petersburg and some northern regions. Strikes on other parts of Russia continued, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he is not authorized to talk publicly.

Video captured a U.S. military transport plane coming in for a landing Tuesday at Moscow's Vnukovo airport, in a flight that the Kremlin initially claimed it had no information about.

Data from the website Flightradar24 showed that the Boeing C-17A Globemaster III left Joint Base Andrews in Maryland early Sunday afternoon on a flight to Riga, Latvia. The aircraft then traveled from Riga to Moscow on Tuesday morning.

The last time a U.S.-registered jet made a direct flight to Russia from Europe was in January when special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, visited Moscow for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine, according to Reuters.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Idaho judge grants Bryan Kohberger two hearings next year as admitted killer seeks to withdraw guilty plea
item.description: Bryan Kohberger won an evidentiary hearing in June 2027 after claiming his defense team convinced him to falsely confess to the Idaho murders.
item.content:encoded:
Convicted quadruple murderer Bryan Kohberger, who admitted to stabbing four University of Idaho students a year before he proclaimed his innocence and asked to withdraw his guilty plea, has been granted two days in court next year as part of his petition for post-conviction relief.

Judge Steven Hippler, who accepted Kohberger's guilty pleas in July 2025, set a status conference for June 3, 2027, and an evidentiary hearing two weeks later on June 17 of that year, according to a court order dated Wednesday.

Prosecutors had asked the judge to dismiss Kohberger's petition without a hearing.

ATTORNEY WHO DEFENDED DC SNIPER SAYS KOHBERGER FACES 'MONUMENTAL UPHILL BATTLE' UNDOING GUILTY PLEA

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the murders of four University of Idaho students — Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin — in a plea deal that spared him from the potential death penalty.

A year later, he asked to withdraw his guilty pleas and proclaimed his innocence in a petition for post-conviction relief.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S POST-CONVICTION RELIEF BID ENABLED BY FLAWED PLEA DEAL, PSYCHOLOGIST ARGUES

Kohberger, in a handwritten petition on July 27, 2026, claimed that he was "convinced to falsely confess" by his high-profile defense team of Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow. He alleged that they failed to tell him about "exculpatory discovery" — hair found at the scene that was not tested for DNA. It was excluded as Kohberger's through a physical analysis.

His new attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

BRYAN KOHBERGER APPOINTED NEW LAWYER AFTER IDAHO MURDERS CASE COSTS TAXPAYERS OVER $8 MILLION

Police found his DNA on a knife sheath recovered from the crime scene in a bed with two of the victims, according to authorities. They also tracked his vehicle coming and going, and forensic investigators were prepared to testify about how. Although he shut his phone off during the murders, the evidence suggested he drove to and from the crime scene anyway.

Separately, Sy Ray, a former expert witness working for Kohberger's defense team, last month alleged that there is additional damaging evidence that investigators hadn't introduced before Kohberger's guilty plea.

Hippler sentenced him to four consecutive terms of life without the possibility of parole, plus another 10 years.

The plea deal required Kohberger to waive his right to appeal. However, that doesn't block him from seeking post-conviction relief, which could potentially reopen the case or result in a new trial.

Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador told Fox News Digital shortly after Kohberger's petition was filed that his office is "ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."

item.title: Atlanta NHL comeback bid takes major step with new arena progress
item.description: Alpharetta's city council narrowly approved redeveloping North Point Mall into a massive entertainment district with a 20,000-seat NHL-ready arena.
item.content:encoded:
There's a lot of buzz around the NHL about the league bringing in 33rd and 34th franchises, and one of those looks set to head to either Austin or Houston.

The leader in the clubhouse for the other is Atlanta (yes, again), and one of the two groups looking to bring a team to town hit a big milestone this week.

The city council in Alpharetta, Georgia, a northern Atlanta suburb, voted 4-3 to approve the redevelopment of the North Point Mall into a mixed-use entertainment district featuring a very large arena capable of being home to an NHL team.

SACRAMENTO MAKES ITS CASE AS MLB'S NEXT EXPANSION CITY, CALLING ITSELF A MARKET TOO BIG TO IGNORE

The proposal was led by real estate and placemaking firm Jamestown for the site owner, New York Life, and in partnership with real estate developer Machete Group, which specializes in this kind of project.

"We are thrilled to have achieved this significant milestone and grateful to the City of Alpharetta, its elected officials, staff, and the community for their thorough review and support of our vision for North Point’s future," Chief Investment Officer at Jamestown Tim Perry said in a statement. "This approval reflects the City’s confidence in the transformative opportunity of the project and in Jamestown’s ability to bring this vision to life. It also positions North Point to become a regional, year-round destination for professional sports, entertainment, and mixed-use experiences, while bringing substantial investment, economic impact, and community benefit."

The plan is for the site to be home to a 20,000-seat arena, which would make it the second-biggest in the league behind only Montreal's Bell Centre.

The site would also be home to a 4,000-seat music hall and performing arts center, a 2,000-seat community hockey rink, a 1,100-seat movie theater, a 35,000-square-foot hotel conference center, and hundreds of rooms across two hotel buildings.

WWE SURVIVOR SERIES: WARGAMES HEADS TO HOUSTON IN NOVEMBER

Interestingly, this is one of two groups looking to build an NHL venue in the area. Another project is being proposed in Forsyth County, just seven miles away, according to FOX 5 Atlanta.

The NHL previously had a presence in Atlanta from 1972 to 1980 with the Atlanta Flames before they moved to Calgary, and then again from 1999 to 2011 with the Atlanta Thrashers before they moved to Winnipeg and became the current version of the Jets.

At the moment, the Atlanta area is home to the ECHL's Atlanta Gladiators, an affiliate of the Nashville Predators, who play in Duluth, Georgia.
